introduction: Xenophon, Cyropaedia 1.3.16–18. 253 Greek words in 5 paragraphs.

The coat dispute and Cyrus’s conversation with Mandane follow Cyropaedia 1.3.16–18. The deliberative questions and closing reflection are composed for this course; neither these speeches nor the scene is an independent record of Persian schooling.

Read once for the argument, then translate paragraph by paragraph. Use the glosses during the first pass; translate the closing paragraph continuously. Submit your connected English translation using the reading submission box.

The vocabulary panel separates new required entries from review words. Paragraph glosses supply additional reading support; a gloss alone does not make a word or an advanced construction a production requirement.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Κῦρος ἔτι παῖς ὢν παρὰ τῷ πάππῳ διέτριβεν. ἡ δὲ μήτηρ Μανδάνη περὶ τῆς παιδείας αὐτοῦ ἠρώτα. οὐ μόνον γὰρ τὸ σῶμα ἀσκεῖν ἔδει τὸν παῖδα, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ δίκαια μανθάνειν. ὁ δὲ Κῦρος ἔλεγεν ὅτι παρὰ τοῖς Πέρσαις ἐμάνθανε κρίνειν καὶ ὅτι ὁ διδάσκαλος πολλάκις αὐτὸν δικαστὴν ἐποίει.

Δύο γὰρ παῖδες περὶ χιτώνων διεφέροντο. ὁ μὲν μέγας παῖς μικρὸν χιτῶνα εἶχεν, ὁ δὲ μικρὸς μέγαν. ὁ οὖν μέγας τὸν τοῦ μικροῦ χιτῶνα ἀφελόμενος τὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἐκείνῳ ἔδωκεν. ἑκάτερος οὕτω χιτῶνα τῷ σώματι ἁρμόττοντα εἶχεν· ἀλλὰ ὁ μικρὸς οὐκ ἐβούλετο τὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἀπολέσαι. οὐ γὰρ ἑκὼν τὴν ἀλλαγὴν ἐποιήσατο.

Ὁ Κῦρος τὸ πρᾶγμα ἐξήταζεν. τί ποιήσω; πότερον τὸ μέγεθος τῶν χιτώνων σκοπῶ ἢ τοὺς κυρίους; ὁ μὲν γὰρ χιτὼν τῷ μεγάλῳ παιδὶ καλῶς ἁρμόττει, ὁ δὲ τῷ μικρῷ. κρίνωμεν οὖν κατὰ τὸ χρήσιμον, ἵνα ἑκάτερος τὸ ἁρμόττον ἔχῃ. ταύτην τὴν κρίσιν ἐποιήσατο, νομίζων ἀμφοτέρους ὠφελεῖν.

paragraphs.greek: Ἡ Μανδάνη τὸν λόγον ἤκουε καὶ περὶ τῶν νόμων διέλεγετο. ὁ γὰρ ἄρχων οὐ πανταχοῦ τὴν αὐτὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχει. ὁ παῖς οὖν μὴ μόνον τὰ τῶν ἰσχυρῶν ἔργα θαυμαζέτω, ἀλλὰ τὸ δίκαιον ἐξεταζέτω. ἀκούσωμεν καὶ τοῦ ἀσθενεστέρου, ἵνα μὴ ἡ δύναμις ἀντὶ τοῦ νόμου κρίνῃ. οὕτως ἡ περὶ δύο χιτώνων ζήτησις εἰς τὴν περὶ ἀρχῆς παιδείαν ἄγει.

reading.translation:
While still a boy, Cyrus was staying with his grandfather. His mother Mandane asked about his education. For the boy needed not only to train his body but also to learn what was just. Cyrus said that among the Persians he learned to judge and that the teacher often made him a judge.

Two boys were disputing about tunics. The large boy had a small tunic, and the small boy a large one. The large boy took the small boy’s tunic and gave him his own. Each thus had a tunic fitting his body; but the small boy did not wish to lose his own. For he had not made the exchange willingly.

Cyrus examined the matter. What should I do? Should I consider the size of the tunics or their owners? One tunic fits the large boy well, the other the small boy. Let us therefore judge by usefulness, so that each may have what fits. He made this judgment, thinking that he was benefiting both.

The teacher did not praise the judgment. What fits is one thing, what is just another. Let us investigate not only which tunic fits well, but also whose it is. Let us not wrong the owner in order to benefit the other person. Someone who takes by force does not thereby become the owner because the possession is useful to him.

Mandane listened to the account and discussed laws. For a ruler does not have the same authority everywhere. Let the boy therefore not merely admire the deeds of the powerful, but examine what is just. Let us listen also to the weaker person, so that power may not judge in place of law. Thus the inquiry about two tunics leads into education about rule.

blocks.title: δίκη and judgment
body: Read these related expressions in the lesson’s argument. δίκη means “judgment, justice”; δίκαιος means “just”; δικαστής means “judge”.
Explain which expression fits an action, a person, or an evaluation. A shared root connects meanings but does not make the words interchangeable in a sentence.

objectives: Introduce the subjunctive as a mood, with its characteristic vowel patterns and present/aorist formation in the assigned regular verbs.
Distinguish present and aorist aspect without treating the subjunctive as an ordinary future tense.
Teach the chapter’s principal uses through deliberation, exhortation, prohibition, and purpose as assigned; distinguish questions about what to do from factual questions.
Identify the clause signal, verb form, subject, and intended meaning. Defer systematic general-clause work to Lesson 39 and the full conditional system to Lesson 44.

sections.title: 1. Present and aorist active subjunctives
body: Mood tells us how a clause presents its action. The subjunctive commonly marks an action envisaged, proposed, or dependent on a purpose or other condition. It is not simply a future tense. In regular active forms, the characteristic vowels are ω and η: λύω, λύῃς, λύῃ, λύωμεν, λύητε, λύωσι(ν). The first singular looks like the indicative, so use context.

The present subjunctive uses the present stem; the first aorist uses the sigmatic aorist stem without an augment: λύσω, λύσῃς, λύσῃ, λύσωμεν, λύσητε, λύσωσι(ν). A second aorist uses its own stem, as λάβω. The present presents an activity as ongoing or repeated; the aorist views it as a whole. Neither stem by itself means present versus past time here.

sections.title: 2. Middle, passive, and contracted forms
body: The present middle/passive subjunctive has λύωμαι, λύῃ, λύηται, λυώμεθα, λύησθε, λύωνται. The first aorist middle has λύσωμαι, λύσῃ, λύσηται, λυσώμεθα, λύσησθε, λύσωνται. Middle voice is interpreted from the verb and context; it does not always mean an action done to oneself.

Aorist passives use the passive stem and active-type endings: λυθῶ, λυθῇς, λυθῇ, λυθῶμεν, λυθῆτε, λυθῶσι(ν). Contract verbs retain contraction: τιμῶ, τιμᾷς, τιμᾷ; ποιῶ, ποιῇς, ποιῇ. Do not classify a form by its last two letters alone: identify stem, voice, mood, person, and clause signal.

sections.title: 3. Deliberation, exhortation, and prohibition
body: A deliberative subjunctive asks what one should do: τί ποιήσω; means “What should I do?” rather than a request for a fact already established. First-person plural exhortations invite a shared action: ἀκούσωμεν, “Let us listen.” The subject is included in the proposal.

A negative exhortation uses μή. A prohibition addressed to another person commonly uses μή with the aorist subjunctive for a prohibited action, or μή with the present imperative for ongoing or habitual conduct. Compare μὴ κλέψῃς and μὴ κλέπτε. This is a useful aspect distinction, not a rule that the aorist always means one moment and the present always means “stop.”

sections.title: 4. Purpose and clause reading
body: A purpose clause explains what an action aims to achieve. In primary sequence, ἵνα, ὅπως, or ὡς can introduce a subjunctive: ἐρωτῶ ἵνα μάθω, “I ask so that I may learn.” The intended result need not actually happen. Negative purpose normally has μή after the purpose conjunction.

Find the main action, purpose signal, subject, and subjunctive. A new subject may appear in the purpose clause. Compare διδάσκω ἵνα ὁ παῖς μάθῃ: I teach, but the child learns. We meet systematic general clauses in Lesson 39 and the full condition system in Lesson 44; do not label every subjunctive clause a purpose clause.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Cyropaedia
body: The coat dispute introduces the work’s larger problem: how does someone learn to govern fairly? Read the childhood episode as a test of judgment that may later matter on an imperial scale. Mandane’s questions expose the difference between confidence and understanding. The useful arrangement of possessions does not itself establish a right to take them.

Its eight books follow Cyrus the Great from education to conquest, imperial organization, and death. This Cyrus is the sixth-century founder of Persian power, not Cyrus the Younger of the Anabasis. The opening question is striking: why do people so often resist rulers, and how could Cyrus secure obedience across so many peoples? Childhood training becomes the starting point for a much larger inquiry into power.

Xenophon combines campaigns, speeches, friendships, rivalries, and domestic stories to explore leadership. Rewards and persuasion stand beside military force; admiration for the ruler sits beside questions about dependence on him. The final account of decline after Cyrus complicates an uncomplicated success story. Read this as a crafted political and educational narrative, not a reliable transcript of sixth-century Persian court life.

Reading invitation: compare the opening discussion of obedience in Book 1 with Araspas’s confidence about desire in Book 5 and its consequences in Book 6. Panthea’s story makes the problem personal: can someone entrusted with power govern himself? Then glance at the close of Book 8. What can a leader build that will survive him? The whole-work link opens Henry Graham Dakyns’s English translation, revised by F. M. Stawell.

sections.title: A judgment with two different questions
body: Imagine seeing only the boys and the sizes of their tunics. Giving each the garment that fits seems sensible. Now add the fact that the larger boy took the smaller boy’s property without consent. A useful allocation and a rightful transfer are no longer the same question. Cyrus’ teacher corrects the question he has answered, not merely his ability to notice size. The story lets a beginner’s mistake become a lesson about the limits of benevolent power.

A tunic also represents labor and resources. Cloth must be produced, maintained, and replaced. The Culture/History banner suggests that material world, but its workshop details are a modern reconstruction. Neither the illustration nor the literary story establishes the precise appearance of a Persian school or garment exchange.

sections.title: Mandane and the education of a ruler
body: Mandane questions Cyrus about what he has learned and about the difference between Persian and Median rule. She is an active participant in the educational argument, rather than a decorative family connection. Yet her voice is presented by a male Greek author writing a shaped account of Cyrus the Great. Keep the literary role and the limits of the evidence together.

Timeline: this story concerns Cyrus the Great in the sixth century BCE. The Cyrus whom Xenophon accompanied in 401 BCE was Cyrus the Younger, a different person. A shared name does not turn the Cyropaedia into a memoir of the Anabasis expedition.

sections.title: Try the judgment twice
body: First allocate the two coats by fit and explain your reason. Then make a second judgment after learning who owned each coat and whether the exchange was voluntary. Write two sentences explaining what changed. You may propose a voluntary exchange, but identify it as your solution rather than an event recorded in the passage.

Translation workshop: translate paragraphs 1–2 with glosses; bracket the subjunctives in paragraphs 3–4; then translate paragraph 5 continuously. In your final version distinguish the source-based episode from the course’s questions about power. What evidence would you still need before declaring an exchange fair?
